titre: Archaeopteryx Was Not First Presented as Darwin's Proof
accroche: Found two years after On the Origin of Species, the London fossil is described by Richard Owen, who sees a bird, not a link.
contenu_vulgarise:
Archaeopteryx is often presented as the fossil Darwin was waiting for: a feathered animal with a long bony tail, discovered in 1861, two years after *On the Origin of Species*. The story of the early years is less clear-cut.

## A Fossil Bought With a Whole Collection

An isolated feather is described in 1861 by Hermann von Meyer. The same year, a nearly complete skeleton comes out of the quarries of Solnhofen, in Bavaria, near Langenaltheim. It belongs to the physician and collector Karl Häberlein. The British Museum buys it in 1862. According to *Earth* magazine, from the American Geosciences Institute, George Waterhouse conducts the purchase, encouraged by Richard Owen, and the deal covers Häberlein's entire collection, 1,756 Solnhofen pieces, for 8,400 Bavarian guldens after more than a year of negotiations. It is therefore not a single fossil that is bought, but a whole collection. The Royal Society places the sale in 1862, only a year after the discovery.

## Owen Sees a Bird

Owen reads his description before the Royal Society on November 20, 1862, and the text appears in the *Philosophical Transactions* in 1863. He sees a bird in it, but not a transitional form: according to *Earth*, he ranks it among the archetypes the Creator had planned. Thomas Huxley, a defender of Darwin, recognizes on the contrary a link between reptiles and birds. The letters of January 1863 show what Darwin is after: the Darwin Correspondence Project's notes specify that on January 5 and 6 he asks which digits of the forelimb detached from the wing to form claws. Falconer replies that the two free digits are those on the radius side, and that the others carried the large feathers, but he warns that his opinion remains approximate.

## Darwin, Cautious

In January 1863, Darwin questions Hugh Falconer about the digits of the fossil's forelimb. Falconer replies on January 9, approximately: he has not been able to examine the fossil as closely as the case requires, and does not think he can do so before the publication of Owen's paper. In the fourth edition of *On the Origin of Species*, whose printing is nearly complete in late May 1866, Darwin cites Archaeopteryx. According to the Darwin Correspondence Project's annotation, he sets it against the idea that all birds appeared suddenly in the Eocene. The argument is modest: an already ancient bird, not yet a demonstration of ancestry.

repere.texte: Owen reads his description of Archaeopteryx before the Royal Society on November 20, 1862; the text appears in 1863. Darwin cites Archaeopteryx in the fourth edition of On the Origin (p. 367), whose printing is nearly complete in late May 1866, against the idea of a sudden appearance of all birds in the Eocene.
repere.source: Darwin Correspondence Project, notes to the letters from Falconer (1863) and to Hooker (1866)

carte.punch: The fossil meant to confirm Darwin was first described as a mere bird.
carte.idee: Archaeopteryx, found in 1861, is bought by the British Museum and described by Richard Owen in 1862. Owen sees a bird, not a link. Darwin cites it in the fourth edition of On the Origin, in 1866, with caution.

quiz.question: How does Richard Owen interpret the London Archaeopteryx in 1862?
choix: As a bird, without seeing a transitional form in it
As a flying reptile close to the pterosaurs
As a missing link between reptiles and birds
As a fake made from a reptile and feathers
quiz.explication: Owen sees a bird, which he ranks among the archetypes planned by the Creator rather than in a transitional series. It is Huxley who reads it as a link between reptiles and birds. Owen took the fossil to be neither a pterosaur nor a fake.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the purchase conducted by George Waterhouse in 1862 for the British Museum include?
choix: Karl Häberlein's entire collection, 1,756 Solnhofen pieces, and not just the Archaeopteryx fossil
Only the Archaeopteryx skeleton, sold separately from the rest of the collection
The isolated feather described by Hermann von Meyer, bought before the skeleton
A collection of fossils bought directly from Charles Darwin
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The deal covers Häberlein's entire collection, 1,756 Solnhofen pieces for 8,400 Bavarian guldens, and not just the Archaeopteryx fossil.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Hugh Falconer reply to Darwin on January 9, 1863, about the digits of Archaeopteryx's forelimb?
choix: That no digit ever detached to form claws
That he examined the fossil in detail and that his answer is definitive
That the two free digits are those on the radius side, the others having carried the large feathers, but that his opinion remains approximate
That he refuses to answer before the publication of Owen's paper
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Falconer replies that the two free digits are those on the radius side and that the others carried the large feathers, while specifying that his examination remains approximate, for lack of having been able to study it more closely.

quiz_supplementaire.question: In what context does Darwin cite Archaeopteryx in the fourth edition of On the Origin of Species?
choix: As definitive proof of the link between reptiles and birds
Against the idea that all birds appeared suddenly in the Eocene
To publicly contradict Richard Owen's interpretation
To announce the discovery of a second complete fossil
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to the Darwin Correspondence Project's annotation, Darwin cites Archaeopteryx against the idea that all birds appeared suddenly in the Eocene, a modest argument rather than a demonstration of ancestry.
